prompt: You read 12 bits and 0.8 mV steps on the datasheet, then expect the console to agree with your meter to a millivolt. Where does that expectation go wrong?
options: Resolution counts the steps; accuracy is where the whole staircase sits
The 0.8 mV figure applies to averaged readings, never to raw ones
The ±50 mV is the trimpot's tolerance rather than the converter's

prompt: Two boards built from the same BOM read tens of millivolts apart at the same knob position, before calibration is applied. What are you seeing?
options: The delay the RC filter adds when you sweep the knob quickly
The per-chip reference, which lands anywhere in a 200 mV window
Noise picked up from the radio while the converter is sampling

prompt: A classmate's readings turn to garbage the moment their firmware brings Wi-Fi up. Why can that not happen on this board?
options: Firmware refuses to open an ADC2 channel and logs a warning instead
The lesson keeps the radio switched off for the whole measurement
The signal is wired to an ADC1 channel in copper, so the trap cannot fire

prompt: Your averaged readings still jump about, and an ohm sweep finds a scratchy patch mid-travel on the pot. Which sourcing call does that vindicate?
options: An open-frame pot cannot span the rail without a series resistor
The cheapest parts are rarely listed under an exact orderable MPN
The knob gets swept constantly, and a worn wiper reads as ADC noise

prompt: This is the leanest BOM in the series: five analog lines. Why so few?
options: The board itself is half the size of the four boards before it
The part under test ships inside the module, so the front end is one source, one filter and one guard
Analog parts are expensive, so the design keeps their count down

prompt: C8 ends up on the pot side of R7 instead of at the pin. Every net still connects. What did that cost you?
options: The filter: the network is R7 into a capacitor at the pin, in that order
Nothing measurable: a capacitor to ground filters the same either way
The pot's usable range, which now stops short of the 3.3 V rail

prompt: D2 clamps AIN rather than ADC_IN. Why there?
options: ADC_IN has no board room left beside the 100 nF capacitor
Strikes arrive where hands and probes touch, so the clamp meets them there
The clamp needs the pot's resistance in series with it to work

prompt: GPIO3 is an ADC1 channel as well. Why is it still the wrong pin for the knob?
options: It belongs to the module's fixed native USB data pair
Its channel number collides with the stored calibration data
It is a strapping pin, so the knob's position at reset could change how the chip boots

prompt: The schematic says the 100 nF belongs at the pin. What does that mean once you are placing parts?
options: The capacitor's pad within millimetres of GPIO1's pad, with R7 immediately upstream
The capacitor on the same net as the pin, which the netlist already guarantees
A wide trace from the capacitor to the pin, so charge arrives quickly

prompt: To save space you run the analog trace alongside the USB pair for a few millimetres. What is the risk?
options: A high-impedance measurement node picks up whatever switches beside it
DRC flags the spacing as a differential-pair clearance violation
The USB pair loses its match and enumeration turns unreliable

prompt: You place RV1 in the middle of the board, hemmed in by other parts. What did that cost?
options: Heat: the pot can no longer shed what the rail puts into it
Clearance: its body now overlaps the pour on the inner layers
The workflow: the lesson is sweep and watch, and you cannot reach the screw while the console is in view

prompt: On the viewer pass, which silkscreen earns the deliberate look on this board?
options: The board name, to confirm the silk font reads at this size
J4's 3V3 / AIN / GND order and RV1's marking, which a probing hand relies on
The antenna keep-out outline, so the assembler leaves it clear

prompt: Why does this lesson ask you to check your multimeter before the boards even arrive?
options: A meter's input resistance loads the pot and shifts the reading
The build log will not accept a run without a calibration record
Bring-up measures a measurer, so the meter is the reference instrument and has to be trusted first

prompt: Three boards' worth of reels are already in your drawer. What should the parts cart hold?
options: The real gaps, counted first: the trimpot and the diode by exact MPN
Fresh reels regardless, since passives drift while they sit unused
Every line bought new, so the front end comes from a single batch

prompt: Which pre-power check does this board add over the earlier builds?
options: A capacitance check on C8, confirming the placed part really is 100 nF
An ohmmeter sweep of RV1, proving smooth wiper travel while the board is cold
A DC voltage reading at J4's AIN pin against the board's ground

prompt: You sweep the knob to each end in turn. How do the two limits differ on the console?
options: Both ends pin flat, one of them at 0 and the other at 4095
The top pins hard at 4095, while the bottom's small codes keep wandering outside the accuracy band
Both ends wander, since the accuracy band covers the whole range

prompt: Your meter reads 1.650 V on AIN while the console's calibrated reading says 1.628 V. Finding or physics?
options: Physics: 22 mV sits inside the ±50 mV band the part is honest to
A finding: 22 mV is 27 codes, far past what 0.8 mV steps allow
A finding: recalibrate in firmware until the two readings agree

prompt: Averaging visibly tightens the stream of readings. What does it leave untouched?
options: The width of the raw wobble, which reads the same either way
The clip at the top, which averaging pushes a little higher
The ±50 mV band: averaging shrinks the random part and never the calibrated staircase's offset
